title: Parvati and the Hermit
hook: Parvati's fierce tapas, and the disguised Shiva's first question: is this within your strength? the body is the first tool of dharma
carry: the body is the first tool of dharma

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna's oil bath at dawn: in Hindu practice, the body is readied for the sacred.

A young woman stands in the summer heat between four fires, with the sun blazing overhead. In winter she stands in icy water. In time she stops eating even fallen leaves. She's Parvati, and she's set out to win Shiva, the great ascetic, by matching him in austerity. Her mother begged her: u, ma, oh, don't, and that, the poet says, is how she got the name Uma. Then one day a young hermit with matted hair walks up and asks a strange first question.
screen: `FOUR FIRES AND THE SUN.` → `HER MOTHER CRIES, 'U, MA.'` → `A HERMIT'S FIRST QUESTION.`

segments.voice: This is Kalidasa's poem, the Kumarasambhava, and the hermit is Shiva in disguise, come to test her. Among his first questions, he asks after her body. Is your austerity within your own strength? For the body, after all, is the first means of dharma: shariram adyam khalu dharma-sadhanam. That half-line is still quoted all over India. Parvati does win him: when she defends Shiva against the hermit's teasing, he drops the disguise and tells her he's hers, won by her tapas. But the poem puts its question first. Here's the teaching. Hinduism prizes tapas, discipline, and it has always warned against crushing the body to get there. In the Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little; it's for the one who is measured in food, play, effort and rest. And he calls fierce self-torture a mistake: it torments the body, he says, and me, who dwells within it. Ayurveda puts the same rule into the daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done to ardha shakti, half of one's strength, and for many people less, and the tradition reads the signs: sweat on the forehead, breath coming through the mouth. That's enough. Today, that's a different idea of effort from the gym wall's no pain, no gain. Training hard is good. Training to break misreads what the body is for. A disciplined Hindu life is strong, regular, and stopped while there's something left.
screen: `THE BODY: FIRST MEANS OF DHARMA` · `TAPAS, WITHOUT CRUSHING THE BODY` · `MEASURED IN FOOD, PLAY, EFFORT, REST` · `ARDHA SHAKTI: HALF STRENGTH`

segments.voice: Sitting tall, breathe in and slowly raise both arms in front of you, as high as is comfortable, and breathe out as you lower them, a few times. If you know Surya Namaskar, the sun salutation many Hindus do in the morning, this is close to its first movement. Notice the breath deepening and the shoulders warming, and stop before it becomes strain, with something left. If you pray, give thanks for the body that does your work.
The daily routine. Its exercise, vyayama, is done to half one's strength, because, as Kalidasa's Shiva says, the body is the first means of dharma.
Your line: the body is the first tool of dharma. Ask Parvati's question: within your strength? Go gently.

sources.ref: Kalidasa, Kumarasambhava 1.26 (her mother's 'u ma', and the name Uma) and canto 5 (Parvati's tapas; the disguised Shiva's question, 5.33: is your tapas within your strength, for the body is the first means of dharma; his self-revealing, 5.86)
Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little, but for the measured) and 17.5–6 (fierce austerities torment the body and the one who dwells within it)
Charaka Samhita, Sutrasthana 7.31–32 (exercise: bodily effort desired for steadiness and strength, to be done in measure; its benefits, including bearing hardship)
Ashtanga Hridaya, Sutrasthana 2.10–11 (benefits of exercise; half strength for the strong in the cooler seasons, less for others)
